items.title: The one way onto the Ladder
items.body: Moksy's published reviewer pages describe a single route onto the Ladder, the same for everybody. First, apply: your Track, how long you have worked in it, your current title and a couple of pieces of work, about ten minutes. Second, sit the Calibration: a blind review of a seeded document (with planted defects) in your own field, 45 to 60 minutes. Everybody sits it, because a level typed into a form is not evidence; what your experience decides is what a pass is worth, setting the rung and the Band you start on, never whether you are asked. Third, get accredited: you hold a live accreditation in your Track. Accreditation is held per Category, so a reviewer can sit on different rungs in different fields. Your first three reviews are read by a senior reviewer before they reach the customer, and they are paid in full at the ordinary rate: the check protects the customer while your record is short, and you are not paying for it. The careers page adds that applying as a reviewer is the job application, there is no separate one, and there is no portal or cover-letter template (careers@moksy.ai is for telling Moksy what you would want to work on); reviews are paid from the first one, so there is no unpaid test; accreditation is calibrated, not granted because someone likes you; the process is the same length for everyone; and when a role opens Moksy looks at who has been reviewing well in that discipline. Source: reviewer-process.json, reviewer-levels.json, careers.json.

questions.prompt: An applicant emails: "I have fifteen years as a solution architect. Can I skip the Calibration, start at the top rung, and how much will I earn?" Write the reply, using only what Moksy has published.
questions.answer: Thank you for your interest. Everybody sits the Calibration, a 45 to 60 minute blind review of a document from your own field with planted defects, because a level typed into a form is not evidence. Your experience does count: it sets what passing is worth, meaning the rung and Band you start on, so a long career does not land you at the bottom. The top rung, Principal, is by invitation on a record Moksy can point at, so it is not somewhere to start. After you are accredited, your first three reviews are read by a senior reviewer before they reach the customer, and they are paid in full at the ordinary rate. On earnings, reviews are priced and paid in MOX, and our payouts page gives worked examples of what reaches a reviewer rather than a promise of volume, so I cannot give you a figure. You can apply in about ten minutes by telling us your Track, how long you have worked in it, your current title and a couple of pieces of work.
questions.rubric: A good answer: says everybody sits the Calibration and explains why (self-declared level is not evidence); says experience sets the rung and Band they start on and that Principal is by invitation; mentions the first three reviews are read by a senior reviewer and paid in full; does not give an income figure or promise (the page gives worked examples, not a promise of volume); mentions the ~10-minute application and what it asks; is courteous and plain. Penalise promising to skip the Calibration, promising a top rung, or quoting an income.

items.title: The five rungs: what each may claim
items.body: The published Levels page shows five rungs and says the table is the rule the claim gate actually reads. Candidate: you have applied and not yet passed the Calibration; a Candidate holds no claim rights of any kind. Contributor: you passed the Calibration; your first three reviews are read by a senior reviewer before delivery and paid in full; you may claim Peer Review, one Section at a time, at Band C1, in your declared Track, one piece of work at a time. Reviewer: those first reviews cleared the bar on quality and on time; Peer Review and Expert Review, Sign-off on a whole Blueprint at C1, Section Reviews at C2, two Tracks and three pieces of work at once. Senior: a sustained record at Reviewer, sampled rather than self-reported; adds Priority Review and direct invitations, Sign-off up to C3, three Tracks, five pieces at once, and may delegate Sections. Principal: by invitation, on a record Moksy can point at; every route, Sign-off to C4, no limit on Tracks, eight at once, and one of the people who checks a Contributor's first three. Bands describe how demanding a piece of work is: C1 Simple, C2 Single system, C3 Complex, C4 Regulated. Concurrency is what a rung most visibly buys. A rung is not bought (no Membership raises your rung, Band or Tracks); it is not permission to take a specific job (the claim gate still checks conflicts, Band and availability); it does not lower the standard; and it does not survive a conflict you failed to declare. Source: reviewer-levels.json.

items.title: The life of a review, and what makes one acceptable
items.body: A review is not a rubber stamp and not a rewrite: it is a set of specific corrections to the parts of a Blueprint that are wrong. Nothing is pushed at a reviewer. Work is claimed from the reviewer's Queue, which holds the jobs their accreditation, Band and availability allow, with the scope, the window and the fee shown before they claim. Leaving a job in the Queue costs nothing; claiming it starts the clock. The reviewer reviews section by section, correcting what is wrong and saying why (vague disagreement is not a correction); the customer then accepts the corrections or pushes back, and accepted corrections are what the reviewer's standing is built from. Fees are released from Escrow once the review is accepted or the customer's response window closes without a dispute. A disputed review goes to a senior reviewer to adjudicate; their decision settles whether the review counts as accepted, and the fee follows it. Peer Review is the free check for a customer on the free Membership: it carries no money, earns MXP, and is where a new reviewer builds a record. What makes a review acceptable, at every rung: it points at a Section and states what is wrong with it; somebody else could verify the correction without taking your word for it; it is returned inside the window the job carries (late work is declined work with extra steps); it is conflict-free; it is proportionate (a minor Blueprint does not need a major rewrite, and a major flaw is not a footnote); and it is the reviewer's own work (a review generated by a model is not a review). If a reviewer disagrees with a whole Blueprint, they say so in the review with reasons: it has to be argued, not asserted. Leaving work does not count against a reviewer; reviewing outside their competence does. Source: reviewer-process.json, reviewer-payouts.json.

questions.prompt: A Contributor's review of a customer's Blueprint says only: "The architecture is weak and the costs look wrong." Explain, in feedback addressed to the reviewer, why this does not meet Moksy's standard, and show what an acceptable version would contain.
questions.answer: Thanks for the review. As written it is not yet a correction. A review points at a Section and states what is wrong with it, and vague disagreement is not a correction. "Weak" and "look wrong" do not tell the customer which Section is affected, why it is wrong, or what would fix it, and nobody else could verify them without taking your word for it. An acceptable version names the Section (for example the hosting and architecture Section) and states the specific problem and the reason, with something checkable: which component is inadequate, what the plan assumes, why that fails, and what to change. For the costs, name the line and the figure you dispute and say what you would expect and why, in a way someone else could verify. Keep it proportionate to the size of the flaw and return it inside the window. If you think the whole premise is wrong, say so with reasons: it has to be argued, not asserted.
questions.rubric: A good answer: explains that the review does not point at a Section, give a reason or offer something verifiable (vague disagreement is not a correction); shows an acceptable version naming a Section, the specific problem, the reason and a checkable fix; mentions proportionality and the window; mentions arguing, not asserting, if disputing the premise; is constructive in tone. Penalise rewriting the Blueprint for them or inventing facts about the Blueprint.

items.title: What a review pays
items.body: As published on the payouts page on 11 October 2026: reviews are priced and paid in MOX, Moksy credit pegged at 1 MOX = $0.01. When a reviewer withdraws, MOX converts to money at the rate Moksy publishes, 125 MOX to £1 "today"; operators can change that rate, and every earnings entry records the rate. MXP is a different thing: it measures progression on the Ladder and is not what a review is paid in. What a job is worth (before the reviewer's share): Peer Review carries no money; a Section Review starts from 75 MOX (about £0.60), with higher floors for thin fields (Security and compliance 105 MOX, Accessibility 90, Cloud 83); a whole Blueprint from 250 MOX (about £2), with Track uplifts of 350, 300 and 275 MOX; an Expert Review is 490 MOX (about £3.90), the floor for any review bought on a paid Membership whatever its scope (a job worth more by scope and Track is charged at the higher of the two); a Priority Review is 1,990 MOX (about £15.90), an Expert Review returned inside 36 hours. What reaches the reviewer: share = job value × the rung's payout share × what the reviewer's Membership leaves. Payout share runs from 0.55 at the first paid rung to 0.95 at the top. The Membership takes 20% on the free one, 12% on Reviewer Pro and 8% on Reviewer Elite. Worked examples on the page: an Expert Review at the first paid rung on the free Membership is about 215 MOX (roughly £1.70); a Priority Review at the first paid rung on the free Membership about 875 MOX (roughly £7); a Priority Review at the top rung on Reviewer Elite about 1,739 MOX (roughly £13.90). The page calls these worked examples, not a promise of volume. Earnings become withdrawable after a hold: 14 days on the free Membership, 7 on Reviewer Pro, 3 on Reviewer Elite. There is no negotiation: what sets a rate is the payout share, the scope, the Track and the Membership. There is no payment for work left in the Queue, withdrawn, or returned outside the window, and Peer Review says it carries no fee before you claim it. The Earnings ledger shows the gross, the deduction and the net for every entry. Source: reviewer-payouts.json.

questions.prompt: A reviewer on the first paid rung, on the free Membership, completes one Expert Review and one Priority Review. Using the published figures, work out what reaches them in MOX and in pounds, how long before they can withdraw, and say what you would honestly tell them about income.
questions.answer: An Expert Review is 490 MOX and a Priority Review 1,990 MOX. At the first paid rung the payout share is 0.55 and the free Membership takes 20%, leaving 80%. Expert Review: 490 × 0.55 × 0.80 = about 215 MOX. Priority Review: 1,990 × 0.55 × 0.80 = about 875 MOX. Together about 1,090 MOX. At the published 125 MOX to £1 that is about £8.70 (roughly £1.70 plus £7). The earnings are withdrawable after the hold, 14 days on the free Membership, and the conversion is at the rate published when they withdraw. Honestly, these are worked examples, not a promise of volume, and the amounts per review are small, so I would not promise an income; the rate can improve by climbing the Ladder (payout share rises to 0.95) and by a Membership that takes less and shortens the hold.
questions.rubric: A good answer: uses 490 and 1,990 MOX with 0.55 share and 80% after the 20% free Membership take; gets about 215 and about 875 MOX (total about 1,090); converts at 125 MOX to £1 to about £8.70 (about £1.70 and £7); states the 14-day hold on the free Membership; is honest that the page gives examples not a promise of volume and does not promise income; may mention that the rate depends on the published conversion and can change, and that climbing the Ladder or a Membership changes the share. Penalise arithmetic errors or any promise of earnings.

items.title: The reviewer code of conduct
items.body: The published code says a reviewer's value is their independence, and sets seven standards. (1) Independence: review the plan in front of you on its merits; do not soften a review to protect a relationship, a future engagement or your acceptance rate, and do not sharpen one to justify a fee; if you cannot be independent, decline, which costs nothing. (2) Conflicts of interest: declare before you accept work, not after. A conflict includes a commercial relationship with the customer, work for a direct competitor of theirs, a personal relationship with somebody named in the plan, or any interest in the tools or suppliers the plan recommends. Disclosure is not disqualification; concealment is. (3) Confidentiality: everything in a customer's plan is confidential; do not reuse it, quote it, show it to a colleague, or feed it into a tool that retains it; confidentiality does not end when the review does. (4) Competence: accept only work you are competent to review, because a confident review from outside your domain is worse than no review. (5) Your own work: a review must be your judgement; using a model to help you read or draft is fine, but submitting a model's output as a review is not, and passing it off ends your account. (6) Conduct towards customers: be direct about what is wrong and civil about who wrote it; contempt is not rigour. (7) Consequences: breaches are reviewed by a senior reviewer or by Moksy; depending on severity the outcome is a correction, a level reduction, suspension from the marketplace, or removal with outstanding fees withheld where the work itself was fraudulent. Source: reviewer-conduct.json.

questions.prompt: A Reviewer-rung reviewer claimed a Section Review and then realises the plan recommends a tool that their employer resells. What should they do, which parts of the code of conduct apply, and what does it cost them?
questions.answer: They should declare the conflict now and decline or stop the review rather than reviewing around it. The code says to declare a conflict before accepting work, not after; a conflict includes any interest in the tools or suppliers the plan recommends, and disclosure is not disqualification while concealment is. Independence applies too: they cannot review the plan on its merits if they have an interest in the recommended tool, and the code says that if you cannot be independent about a piece of work you decline it, and declining costs nothing. Leaving work does not count against them, whereas hiding the conflict would be a breach with consequences ranging from a correction to a level reduction or suspension, reviewed by a senior reviewer or Moksy.
questions.rubric: A good answer: tells them to declare the conflict and decline/stop; cites the conflicts-of-interest rule (declare before accepting; supplier/tool interest is a conflict; disclosure is not disqualification, concealment is); cites independence and that declining costs nothing; notes that leaving work does not count against them; mentions the consequences of concealment (correction, level reduction, suspension; reviewed by a senior reviewer or Moksy). Penalise advice to continue quietly or to 'review fairly anyway'.

items.title: Disciplines, careers and what Moksy will not do
items.body: The careers page says every job at Moksy starts with a reviewer account: Moksy works on the problem that most software fails in the specification, not the implementation, and the way in is to do the work first. Applicants apply as reviewers, review real plans, and Moksy hires from the people already doing it well: a CV says what somebody says they can do, while a review shows what they actually caught on a real plan in their own field. The page lists fourteen disciplines it hires into, each at junior, mid-weight and senior levels: Solution architect, Technical lead, Backend engineer, Frontend engineer, Data engineer, DevOps engineer, Site reliability engineer, Security engineer, QA engineer, UX designer, UI designer, Product manager, Delivery manager and Business analyst. Some people are offered a job in weeks; some stay reviewers because they prefer it, and both are a good outcome. What Moksy says it will not do: ask for unpaid work as a test, grant accreditation because it likes you, skip the details for somebody it wants quickly, hire you a level above where you are so it can pay below it, or keep a vacancy open it has no intention of filling. Source: careers.json.

items.title: Where documents disagree: confirm before quoting
items.body: Support and coordinators should quote the published pages, and a few documents disagree. As read on 11 October 2026: (1) Rungs: the published Levels page shows five rungs (Candidate, Contributor, Reviewer, Senior, Principal), while Moksy's internal lexicon lists six named rungs ending in Fellow; quote the published five and say you will confirm whether a further rung exists. (2) Sign-off: the published table says a Reviewer may Sign-off a whole Blueprint at Band C1 and a Senior up to C3, while the lexicon says a Senior may Sign-off a whole Blueprint; the published table is, in its own words, the rule the claim gate actually reads. (3) Lists of fields: the careers page lists fourteen disciplines, the payouts and levels pages talk about Tracks such as Security and compliance, Public sector, Healthcare, Data and AI, Accessibility and Cloud, and an internal application builder in the repository describes 25 roles at eight levels; do not tell an applicant how many fields exist, say the application asks for a Track or discipline and the categories they can judge, and confirm which list the live form uses. (4) Prices: an August 2026 launch-promo proposal reported that internal review price tables disagreed; the payouts page publishes figures and says they are what the platform charges and pays today, but also that operators can change the conversion rate, so quote them as published and dated, and never as a promise. (5) Adjudication: pages say a senior reviewer adjudicates disputes; do not name a rung. (6) Pay for the first three reviews: the pages say a new reviewer's first three reviews are paid in full, while the Contributor row lists only Peer Review, which the payouts page says carries no money; do not tell an applicant what their first three reviews will pay, say you will confirm which work they are and what it pays. Source: reviewer-levels.json, reviewer-payouts.json, careers.json, MOKSY_LEXICON.md, MOKSY_REVIEWER_ONBOARDING.md, LAUNCH_PROMO_SPEC.md.
